title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E449 (Novi Commentarii 18, 1774) builds the theory of residues of powers modulo a prime P from first principles. Its goal is to prove existence and properties of what Euler names 'radices primitivae' a few paragraphs later (§18). On this page he collects examples and two elementary reductions.

§12 continues the worked example P = 7 from §11, where a = 3 gave the full cycle. It lists the residues of a^n mod 7:
- a = 2: period 1, 2, 4, of order 3.
- a = 4: period 1, 4, 2, of order 3.
- a = 5: period 1, 5, 4, 6, 2, 3, of order 6.
So for P = 7 only 3 and 5 generate all nonzero residues. Together with a = 1 (order 1) and a = 6 = −1 (order 2) from §10, every base mod 7 is now covered. The orders 1, 2, 3, 3, 6, 6 illustrate that orders divide P − 1 and that there are φ(6) = 2 generators, though Euler does not say this here.

§13: if a ≡ a' (mod P), then a^n ≡ a'^n (mod P), since (a+P)^n ≡ a^n by the binomial theorem. So the residue sequence depends only on a mod P, and it suffices to take 0 < a < P. In modern terms, the order is a function on (Z/PZ)*.

§14: just as residues may be taken negative so that |residue| ≤ P/2 (the least absolute residue system of §9), the base may be negative. The residues of (−a)^n are those of a^n with alternating signs: 1, −α, β, −γ, …

§15: base −a gives the same residues as base P − a, since −a ≡ P − a. So the sequences for bases a > P/2 follow from those for bases a < P/2 by sign alternation. This is the reduction g ↦ −g in (Z/PZ)*; it implicitly links the order of −a to the order of a (same order if the order of a is even, double it if the order is odd), though Euler does not state this here.

The page serves as the empirical motivation for §§16–18 (complete/incomplete series; the question whether primitive roots always exist).

ideas.what: Tables of power residues mod 7 for bases 2, 4, 5, showing periods of length 3, 3, 6.
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (power residues, 1750s–1770s); systematized by Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), Sect. III
ideas.where_published: E262 (Theoremata circa residua ex divisione potestatum relicta), E449, and Euler's Vollständige Anleitung zur Algebra

ideas.what: The residue sequence depends only on the base modulo P.
Use of negative bases and least absolute residues; base −a is equivalent to P − a, so the cases a > P/2 reduce to a < P/2.
ideas.modern_name: least absolute residue system; symmetry g ↦ −g in (Z/PZ)*

deep.surprise_reason: Elementary worked examples and trivial reductions that motivate Euler's well-known introduction of the term 'primitive root' in E449. All of it is standard and well documented.
transcription_corrections: No substantive errors. In §14 the image shows the residue sequence 1, −α, β, −γ, δ, −ε, ζ, −η, consistent with the transcription.
§15 reads 'a < ½P'; the transcription renders it correctly as a<\frac{1}{2}P.
